un-ga-res-a-69-64:

The text holds that swapping facts on these steps builds grasp and trust between states. It notes the two-way gain: calmer regions make arms cuts easier, and arms cuts calm regions in turn. Past votes from 2004 on are recalled as the base for the call.
un-sc-res-364: Resolution 364 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 1966. un-sc-res-1764: Under the number 1764, a formal decision of the fifteen-member Security Council survives through a Wikisource transcription of the record. cia-0000136564: One of the Spanish documents of Brigade 2506 is dated 2 November 1960, a date shared by several records in this release. un-ga-res-52-164:

The text came out of the fifty-second session; catalog copies dated 1998 reflect the year it opened for signature. States had spent years building law piece by piece against attacks on the public.

The treaty makes it a crime to set off bombs in public places, state buildings, and transport systems with intent to kill or cause great damage. Signers must try offenders found on their soil or hand them over for trial elsewhere. It carved out no excuse for such attacks. The convention took effect in 2001 and joined a growing web of anti-terror law.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d64: On October 27, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek, less than a month before the two men were to meet at Cairo. The letter is Document 64 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Keeping China's leader close was a steady task for Washington that fall. The record supplies the date and the names and leaves the subject to the text. It is part of the Foreign Relations series' road to the Cairo Conference.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d164: The British delegation to the Moscow Conference set down a memorandum dated October 24, 1943, preserved as Document 164 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Delegations traded such papers to state a position in writing where speeches might blur it, and the American editors kept this British text among their own files. The record gives the source and the date. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series' Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d264: A luncheon meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943 between General Marshall and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. Later that afternoon Marshall reported to the Combined Chiefs of Staff on a discussion with Chiang about proposed operations in the Southeast Asia Command. The editors presume that discussion took place at this luncheon. The Stilwell Papers show that Stilwell and Madame Chiang were also present. Where the luncheon was held is not indicated.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d364:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 29 November 1943, at half past ten in the morning, record the first three-power military session. General Sir Alan Brooke leads, running through the war as the British see it, with General Marshall invited to interrupt where he disagrees.

Brooke's theme is keeping German divisions pinned down during the five or six months before Overlord can sail, at the earliest on 1 May. In Italy, amphibious hooks around the flanks should drive the Germans north of Rome and wreck the eleven or twelve divisions in the south. In Yugoslavia, where he counts twenty-one German and eight Bulgarian divisions, the Partisans should get arms and air help to deepen German troubles. Turkey's entry, he adds, holds great military advantage, whatever the politics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d464:
John J. McCloy, the Assistant Secretary of War, wrote to John Gilbert Winant, the American ambassador in London, on December 2, 1943. The letter falls between the Tehran Conference, which had ended the day before, and the Second Cairo Conference, which opened on December 4. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

McCloy was one of the War Department's central fixers, and Winant was Washington's man at the center of the British war effort. Their exchange belongs to the back-channel traffic that kept the alliance running while the leaders traveled. Readers see how business moved between Washington and London even at the height of summit season.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d564:
Harry Dexter White, assistant to the Secretary of the Treasury, wrote this memorandum on August 13, 1944. White was the Treasury's chief technical mind and a main designer of the postwar monetary system agreed at Bretton Woods that summer. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

White's papers matter because the peace was being designed in economic offices while armies fought. Questions of money, trade, and Germany's economic future ran from Tehran's discussions into the Quebec Conference that autumn. For readers, this memorandum shows the Treasury's hand in that design work, written by the official who more than any other shaped America's postwar financial plans.
frus-1944-quebec-d64:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Second Quebec Conference. The two men were in the same city, yet the written habit held. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Letters exchanged inside a conference fixed points between sessions and carried proposals too formal for talk. Churchill, installed at the Citadel with Roosevelt, used paper as he always did. For readers, an opening-day message shows the conference starting in the leaders' own words, at the summit remembered for the Morgenthau Plan and the final division of the war's work.
frus-1944-quebec-d164:
Abbot Moffat, chief of the Division of Southwest Pacific Affairs, sent Hull a short covering note on September 8, 1944. It introduces the attached memorandum for the president on Indochina and Southeast Asia, the long paper that follows it in the volume. Moffat explains why policies toward Indochina appear inside a broader Southeast Asia paper.

The policies, he writes, were included to stress correlating Indochina with the other regions of Southeast Asia. They stated the objectives the department's European, Far Eastern, and Near Eastern offices agreed were most desirable. If Churchill raised the subject at Quebec, the president would have them before him. The department also hoped for basic guidance to develop its own policies and procedures.
frus-1944-quebec-d264:
One sentence kept the Octagon basic policies from full agreement, and the secretaries' note C.C.S. 654/8 of September 12, 1944, isolates it. Every other policy for the final report to Roosevelt and Churchill had been settled informally before the conference. The exception was paragraph 6(i), on reorienting forces from Europe to the Pacific as a matter of highest priority.

The British text spoke of regard to other inescapable commitments. The American text said agreed commitments instead. The difference mattered. Britain feared being trapped by promises; America feared unilateral excuses. The Combined Chiefs were asked to decide. Their eventual compromise kept both words: agreed and/or inescapable.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d64:
President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin on 22 January 1945 to settle press rules for the conference code-named Argonaut. His short top secret telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It carries the plan already agreed with Churchill.

Roosevelt says he has decided to have no press representatives at the meeting. Only a small group of uniformed photographers from the American Navy will take the pictures the leaders want. He notes that Churchill agrees. Stalin's reply, quoted in the editors' note, raised no objections and said the same answer had gone to the Prime Minister.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d164:
The Polish ambassador brought his government's latest terms to Washington on 22 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew sent them to the President the next day with a cool judgment. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, finds no real basis for an approach to Moscow in them.

The London Poles would rather leave frontiers until the war ends. But they will talk now, if gains in the north and west make up for losses in the east. They seek an alliance with Moscow inside the new world body. They refuse one-sided solutions and claim the right to order their own home life. If Moscow will not negotiate, they propose an inter-allied military commission to run local rule in Poland for those loyal to London.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d264:
The Joint Staff Planners sent the chiefs a fresh report on Russia and Japan on 18 January 1945. Their paper, J. C. S. 1176/6, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It was drawn up on the planners' own initiative, and a memorandum by General Arnold rides with it as an enclosure.

The coming allied staff conference at Malta, the report begins, offers a favorable chance to advance American planning. That planning rests on Russian participation in the war against Japan. General Deane's recent talks in Moscow had aimed at the information and agreements the planners need. They had not yet been able to win them. The report therefore goes to the Joint Chiefs for their consideration, days before the President's party sails for the Crimea.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d364: The Joint Chiefs asked the President to intervene in person in this short memorandum of February 6, 1945. They judged it necessary to win Stalin's approval for a meeting with the Soviet staff. The subject was details of possible Soviet participation in the war against Japan. They suggested Roosevelt speak to Stalin to obtain his agreement. An endorsement on the paper records that Admiral Leahy delivered it to the President that afternoon, at 4:15. The few lines trace how a staff question became a leader's errand.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d464:
Hiss's notes of the final foreign ministers' meeting, February 11, 1945, return to the question of credit. Bridges reported on the communiqué text. Molotov relayed Stalin's view: the communiqué should say what was agreed on voting, not that the President's proposal had been adopted. No other place, Molotov noted, said on whose initiative a step was taken.

Stettinius answered that the point had been discussed that morning with Stalin and the President present. It would be very hard for him to agree to strike the reference. Molotov replied there had been no agreement on this special point. The notes break off mid-bargain, with the wording — and the credit — still contested.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d64:
Churchill proposed a royal visit to Berlin in telegram number 92 to President Truman, sent June 15, 1945. It is document 64 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. King George VI would be in France and Germany inspecting his troops while the Big Three met, and he wished to spend a day in Berlin.

Churchill's plan has the King take no part in the talks. He would lunch with the Russians if Stalin agreed, then dine in the British sector with Truman and Stalin as fellow heads of state, and leave early the next day. The King would also hand out decorations to Allied officers. Churchill says he has sent the same news to Stalin and asks Truman's view so he can advise the King.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d164:
Secretary Stettinius commented on the draft American agenda from San Francisco on June 22, 1945. His telegram to Grew is document 164 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It works through the items in Noyes's list of June 20, point by point.

Stettinius asks whether free access for foreign correspondents in places like Yugoslavia, Poland, and Czechoslovakia has been considered. On Italy, he wants the item on joining the United Nations moved to last place, and asks whether abolishing the Advisory Council for Italy should be raised. On international bases, he advises that the United States not take the lead in proposing discussion, though the delegation should be ready if others raise it. The comments show the agenda being sharpened at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d264:
A briefing paper traced the long history of international control of the Danube, dated July 6, 1945. The paper is document 264 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gave Truman's staff the legal background for a question the settlement would raise: who governs Europe's greatest river.

The principles began with the Treaty of Vienna in 1815: navigation free to all nations, no charges beyond the cost of upkeep, and rules set by common consent of the river states. The Treaty of Paris in 1856 applied them to the Danube and created a European Commission to run its maritime section. After the First World War the Danube was declared an international river. By 1945 the Soviet Union held both banks of the lower river and meant to run it alone, which the West resisted.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d364:
Frustration boils over in Pauley's letter of July 3, 1945, to Maisky, chairman of the Reparations Commission in Moscow. For the third time, Pauley writes, Maisky had put off the Commission's full meeting. The meeting was to discuss the Soviet proposal set out in Maisky's own Memorandum No. 2, the plan named in the Crimea Protocol.

The American delegation, Pauley notes, had now waited twenty-two days in Moscow. It had not received a single figure to support the Soviet proposal. Nor had Moscow tried to explain the plan's basis to the Americans or, so far as he knew, the British. The letter is a formal protest against allied stalling.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d464:
Italy is redefined as an American interest in an undated briefing book paper on policy toward that country. The objective, it states, is to strengthen Italy economically and politically. A stronger Italy could withstand the forces that threaten to sweep her into a new totalitarianism. The paper lists those forces one by one.

They include economic distress and national humiliation. They include doubt about British intentions, and about America's readiness to carry out a friendly policy. They include Soviet power, shown in Tito's nearly successful move in Venezia Giulia, a well organized Communist party, and no real experience of democratic government. American troops, it notes, are being withdrawn, and with them a sense of protection.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d564:
A secret priority wire from Belgrade charge Harold Shantz reached Washington on June 21, 1945. It is document 564 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports the signing of the Duino military deals and the gap left in them.

Shantz cites a British colonel who said the deals were signed without article 3 of the Belgrade agreement. The Yugoslavs meant to raise that point again at government level. They hoped to have their liberation committee named the sole agency under Allied military government. Shantz adds that the Yugoslav press twists the U.S. stand, since the Belgrade text was never published there. He suggests Washington and London issue a joint statement of facts and broadcast it into Yugoslavia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d664:
Ambassador Caffery described a British bid to read Soviet motives on Tangier from Paris on July 4, 1945. His secret wire is document 664 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports a talk with Peake, head of the British team at the talks.

joly-dialogue-aux-enfers-1864:
Maurice Joly, a French lawyer, wrote this sly book in Brussels in 1864. Its title means a talk in hell between Machiavel and Montesquieu, in French. Joly aimed his wit at Napoleon III, whose rule he held to be a despot's craft in a new dress.

In twenty five talks, Machiavel lays out how a modern despot can rule by law, press, and fear. Montesquieu makes the case for free rule, and is beat down point by point in the game. The book gained a dark fame when the fake Protocols stole its lines years later.
swedenborg-divine-providence-1764:
Divine Providence, from 1764, rounds out Swedenborg's core set of faith books. Emanuel Swedenborg wrote it in Latin late in his long life. It stands with Heaven and Hell and Divine Love and Wisdom. The theme is how God guides the world and each soul in it.

Swedenborg holds that God lets men go free, yet steers all ends to good. Ill deeds are let be, he says, lest free will die. He tells how prayer, chance, and pain fit the great plan. The book gives the calm core of his thought on God's care.
verne-journey-centre-of-the-earth-1864:
Jules Verne wrote A Journey to the Centre of the Earth in 1864. F. A. Malleson gave the tale its English dress used here. A German sage finds an old note that tells of a path down. The note points to a peak in Iceland with a shaft at its heart.

The sage, his kin, and a stout guide climb down through old lava tubes. They find a vast cave sea, lit by strange light, with live beasts of the old world. Storms, thirst, and a blocked path tax their strength to the end. The tale is the great subterranean trip of the age.
walpole-castle-of-otranto-1764:
Horace Walpole wrote The Castle of Otranto in 1764. He first said it was a tale turned from old Italian print. The tale is set in a grim pile in the south of Italy. Prince Manfred holds the pile by a claim of thin right.

A vast helm falls from the sky and crushes Manfred's son on his wed day. Portraits sigh, statues bleed, and a hid curse drives all the fates. Walpole's brief tale set off the whole Gothic line in prose. Its stock of ghosts, tyrants, and hid sins still feeds tales now.
lucretius-nature-of-things-munro-1864:
Lucretius wrote On the Nature of Things in Latin verse in the first century BC. H. A. J. Munro, a Cambridge scholar, gave it a landmark English form in 1864. His version pairs a close prose sense with deep notes on the text.

The poem teaches the creed of Epicurus in six strong books. All things, it says, are atoms and void, and gods do not rule us. Soul dies with body, so fear of death is folly. Munro's work let Victorian readers meet this bold, calm poem. His Latin text and notes set a high bar for scholars.
thoreau-maine-woods-1864:
Henry David Thoreau's The Maine Woods saw print in 1864, after his death, a wilderness narrative set. The book gathers his three Maine trips of 1846, 1853, and 1857 into one posthumous volume for readers. Many call it the founding text of American wilderness writing in the modern sense of the craft.

Thoreau climbs Katahdin and feels nature raw, savage, and not made for man at all there. With Penobscot guides, above all Joe Polis, he canoes lakes and reads moose, pine, and rapid. Polis's skill and lore correct the Concord man's bookish pride in some of the finest pages here. Logging camps and dams raise his fear that Maine's wilds will fall to the axe for profit. The book's awe at untamed land helped seed the American conservation movement after him.
newman-apologia-pro-vita-sua-1864:
John Henry Newman wrote Apologia Pro Vita Sua in 1864 to answer a public charge that he had been dishonest about his beliefs. Newman had led the Oxford Movement within the Church of England, then joined the Roman Catholic Church in 1845. The book defends that path as one of conscience, not deceit.

He traces his thought step by step, from early Calvinist leanings through his Anglican years to his reception at Rome. The honesty and music of the prose won over even readers who shared none of his faith. It stands as the defining religious memoir of Victorian England.
john-cross-dark-night-soul-lewis-1864:
John of the Cross was a Spanish Carmelite friar who was jailed by his own order for backing reform. In prison he began the poem that his Dark Night of the Soul, in Lewis's 1864 translation, explains line by line. The poem and its commentary treat the soul's purgation, its cleansing by loss.

John describes two nights: one strips the senses of their cravings, the other strips the spirit of its false comforts. The dryness believers fear, he argues, is often growth disguised as abandonment by God. Few books map the hard middle of the spiritual life with such precision and mercy.
locke-two-treatises-government-1764:
John Locke's Two Treatises of Government appears here in the 1764 printing, which carries Locke's final corrections. Locke wrote the work in the years around the Glorious Revolution of 1688. It became the charter text of modern constitutional thought in the English-speaking world.

The First Treatise demolishes Robert Filmer's claim that kings rule by divine right as Adam's heirs. The Second builds government on natural rights, property, and the consent of the governed. When rulers break trust, Locke argued, the people may resist. Those claims fed the American and French revolutions. This printing preserves the form in which the eighteenth century read its political bible.
whittier-in-war-time-1864:
John Greenleaf Whittier published In War Time, and Other Poems in 1864, while the Civil War still raged. Whittier, a Massachusetts Quaker, had spent thirty years as abolitionism's bard, editing antislavery papers and risking mobs. This volume is his wartime voice at full power.

The poems cheer Union soldiers, mourn the dead, and demand emancipation as the war's true purpose. Barbara Frietchie, his most famous ballad, tells of an old Maryland woman waving the Union flag at Stonewall Jackson's troops. Other pieces honor nurses, chaplains, and the enslaved people walking to freedom. Whittier's plain Quaker verse spoke to farmhouses and camps alike. The collection stands as the home front's own record of the war years.
cieza-travels-peru-markham-part-1-1864:
Pedro Cieza de León came to the Americas as a teenage soldier and spent years walking Peru with a notebook. His Crónica del Perú of 1553, in Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society translation of 1864, forms Part One of The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de León. The travels themselves cover 1532 to 1550, from first landfalls to the wars of the conquerors.

Cieza describes the Inca road system, cities, and peoples as the first European to survey them with care. He asked questions everywhere and wrote down what the Andean world told him. His chronicle became the great eyewitness record of the Inca conquest. Few sources bring a reader so close to Peru at the moment of its fall.
burton-mission-gelele-vol1-1864:
Richard Burton went to Dahomey in West Africa in 1863 as Britain's envoy to King Gelele. Volume One of A Mission to Gelele, published in 1864, tells of the trip and the court. Burton was already famed for his pilgrimage to Mecca in disguise.

His orders were to press Gelele to end human sacrifice and the slave trade. Burton records the Fon kingdom's army, its famous women soldiers, the Amazons of Abomey, and court rites in close detail. He is frank, curious, and often harsh in judgment. The volume is firsthand ethnography from a kingdom few Europeans had entered.
burton-mission-gelele-vol2-1864:
Volume Two of Burton's Mission to Gelele completes his 1864 account of Dahomey. Burton had spent months at Gelele's court at Abomey, delivering Britain's message. What he saw there changed few British minds but filled two vivid volumes.

This volume treats the customs of the Fon people: festivals, sacrifices, oaths, and the palace guard of women. Burton adds notes on language, trade, and the slave ports of the coast. His mission failed in its aims, as he admits with dry irritation. The ethnography survived the diplomacy, and historians still mine his close, if biased, reporting. A route map and word lists support the main narrative.
speke-what-led-discovery-nile-1864:
John Hanning Speke published What Led to the Discovery of the Source of the Nile in 1864 to defend his great claim. Speke had traveled with Burton in 1857 and 1859 and found Lake Victoria. He argued the lake was the Nile's source, and Burton disputed him.

Speke tells how the expedition split, how he reached the lake, and why he trusted his reading of the land. The feud with Burton, once his close partner, runs bitterly under the narrative. Speke died in a shooting accident the day before a planned public debate. His lake was later confirmed as the source he claimed.
plos-pone-0003464:
Shinya Hoshikawa and co-authors studied how a nerve insulation gene is switched on in 2008. Schwann cells wrap nerves with a fatty coat called myelin. A protein named MAG appears in those cells before wrapping begins. That timing hints MAG helps start the wrapping process.

What turns the MAG gene on was unknown before this work. The team studied the gene's promoter, its start control region. A protein called RING finger protein 10 proved to regulate that switch. Naming the regulator clarifies how myelin formation gets under way. Myelin loss underlies many nerve diseases, so its first steps draw wide interest.
plos-pone-0003564:
Andrea Puhar and co-authors studied anthrax edema toxin in immune cells for this 2008 paper. The toxin is an enzyme that raises cyclic AMP inside host cells. It works near the cell nucleus, the perinuclear region. Its molecular action was still poorly understood.

The team used Jurkat T cells to track the toxin's signaling. It modulated PKA- and CREB-dependent pathways in two phases. Early and late waves hit the cell in sequence. That timed pattern helps explain how anthrax disrupts host defenses. Anthrax is also feared as a weapon, which adds weight to toxin studies.
plos-pone-0003664:
Joseph N. Brown, James J. Kohler, Carter R. Coberley, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Macrophages are long-lived immune cells where HIV-1 can hide for years. They also form a bridge between the body's first defenses and its targeted ones.

The team asked whether HIV-1 switches macrophages on through Toll-like receptors, the usual alarm sensors. They found activation that does not depend on those receptors. The result shows the virus can stir the very cells it lives in by another route, which matters for clearing hidden reservoirs.
plos-pone-0003764:
Maria Manich, Oliver Knapp, Maryse Gibert, and colleagues published this toxin study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Clostridium perfringens makes many toxins that cause severe disease in people and animals. Its delta toxin is one of three blood-cell-destroying toxins released by some strains. The team compared it with its relatives.

Delta toxin proved sequence-related to beta toxin, NetB, and pore-forming toxins of Staphylococcus. Yet it behaves differently in function from those cousins. The kinship reveals a shared pore-punching design behind diverse bacterial weapons, with each tuned to its own targets.
plos-pone-0003864:
J. Greg Doheny, Randy Mottus, and Thomas A. Grigliatti published this genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Chromosomes end in telomeres, protective caps required for chromosome integrity and tied to aging and cancer. The chromatin at telomeres mixes traits of silent and active regions. Genes placed near those ends can be quieted.

The authors describe this telomeric position effect as a third silencing mechanism in eukaryotes. It works beyond the two silencing systems already established in the field. The proposal adds a distinct tool to the known ways cells hush genes by location.
plos-pone-0003964:
Laura W. Harris, Matthew Wayland, Martin Lan, and co-authors sampled tiny brain blood vessels in schizophrenia in 2008. Past studies hinted the schizophrenic brain gets too little energy. Other work found faults in the brain's smallest vessels in patients. Both clues point toward the cerebral microvasculature.

Their PLOS ONE article used laser capture to cut out those vessels precisely. Gene activity in the captured tissue could then be read cleanly. The method separates vessel signals from surrounding brain cells. Findings here may link blood flow and energy supply to schizophrenia. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004064:
Matthew C. Walsh, Gregory K. Kim, Paul L. Maurizio, and co-authors studied an immune adapter protein in 2008. TRAF6 carries signals from interleukin-1 and related receptor families. Its ring-shaped domain can build ubiquitin chains that switch signals on. Those chains were believed essential for its signaling role.

Their PLOS ONE article reports TRAF6 works without tagging itself. Activation of NF-kappaB and MAPK paths proceeded without autoubiquitination. The result separates TRAF6's adapter job from its enzyme job. Immune models must now explain signaling without the assumed chains. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004164:
William Agudelo and colleagues published this theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adaptive immunity begins when class II MHC molecules present small protein fragments, called peptides, to immune cells. The team studied one such pairing: a class II human leukocyte antigen molecule holding a peptide from myelin basic protein, a protein of nerve insulation.

Using theory and modelling, they asked how changes in the peptide reshape the electrostatic landscape, the pattern of electric charge, across the complex. That landscape guides how immune receptors read the pairing. The work may help explain how small peptide changes can tilt the immune system toward attack, as in multiple sclerosis.
plos-pone-0004264:
Boris Shorning and colleagues published this gut study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lkb1 is a tumour suppressor kinase involved in many processes across the body. The team examined what its loss does to intestinal homeostasis, the gut's steady state. They focused on secretory cell development, since Lkb1 is strongly expressed there.

They report that Lkb1 deficiency alters the differentiation of goblet and Paneth cells in the small intestine. These two cell types make mucus and antimicrobial defences, so their misdevelopment changes gut protection. The finding links a cancer gene to the everyday upkeep of the intestine.
plos-pone-0004364:
Mayke Oesterholt and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mutations in the dhfr and dhps genes are linked to failure of sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine treatment. They are also linked to gametocyte carriage, the stage of the parasite that infects mosquitoes. This may boost the spread of drug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, as shown before for chloroquine resistance.

The team studied gametocytes too few to see under a microscope, in western Kenya. They asked whether these hidden carriers pass on drug-resistant parasites. Invisible carriers could silently keep drug resistance spreading after treatment campaigns. A microscope misses these carriers.
plos-pone-0004464: In 2009, Johansson, Jonasson, and Gyllensten linked a hormone receptor to height. Extended haplotypes in the GHRHR gene tracked with human stature. The growth-hormone receptor's variants nudged height. The finding maps normal height genetics. The gene was known in rare dwarfism.
plos-pone-0004564: In 2009, Clement, Santos, and Desmouliere warned of a palm's shrinking wild home. Ecological adaptation of wild peach palm and deforestation-mediated extinction risk were studied. The Arc of Fire threatened wild stands. The work guides in-situ conservation. The palm feeds people.
plos-pone-0004664: In 2009, Vij, Mazur, and Zeitlin found a faulty salt channel fueling lung inflammation. CFTR negatively regulated NFκB-mediated innate immune response. The broken channel let inflammation rage unchecked. The finding maps cystic fibrosis biology. The runaway signaling leads to IL-8.
plos-pone-0004764: In 2009, Popp, Jaenisch, and Witte mapped stroke damage zones in rats anew. Ischemic regions in a rat stroke model were identified. The dead core and penumbra emerged clearly. The study maps stroke biology wiring. The damage dimension is spatio-temporal indeed.
french-art-of-distillation-1664:
John French teaches distillation in The Art of Distillation, from 1664, a great English manual of the craft. Stills draw out the virtues of plants, minerals, and animals drop by drop. Waters, oils, and spirits for medicine fill his practical, workmanlike pages of recipes and furnace lore for the laboratory.

French writes for the working chemist of the seventeenth century here. Herbs for the sick, metals for the seeker, all pass through his alembics. The book blends alchemy's aims with a tradesman's plain method throughout. It served as the chemist's handbook before chemistry had the name, a bridge between the spagyric art of Paracelsus and the science that followed.
lbj-civil-rights-remarks-1964:
Lyndon B. Johnson spoke on signing the Civil Rights Bill on July 2, 1964. His short remarks mark the century's greatest civil rights law. The Texan president signs with plain words and a sober air.

Johnson praises the long fight that brought the bill to his desk. He knows the act may cost his party the South for years. Triumph and hard political realism share his brief, grave statement. The remarks close a legislative battle that had filled the spring. They stand as the spoken capstone of a landmark in American law history. Johnson signed with dozens of pens, handing them out as keepsakes.
civil-rights-act-1964:
The 88th Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 after fierce debate. All eleven titles of the full text stand in this record. Segregation in public places is banned outright by its terms.

Hiring bias is outlawed across the land in the act's strong clauses. Hotels, theaters, lunch counters, and schools must open on equal terms. The law broke the legal back of Jim Crow in the South. Long filibusters and street marches both stand behind its hard passage. The century's greatest legislative win for equality reshaped daily American life at once. Its enforcement clauses gave the paper rights real teeth in court.
warren-commission-report-1964:
President Lyndon Johnson set up the Warren Commission days after President John Kennedy was shot in Dallas in November 1963. Chief Justice Earl Warren led the inquiry, which worked for ten months with a large staff. Its report, issued in September 1964, runs to 888 pages with volumes of evidence behind it.

The commission concluded that Lee Harvey Oswald fired the shots that killed Kennedy, and that he acted alone. It also found that Jack Ruby acted alone when he killed Oswald on live television. Doubts about those findings began at once and have never faded. The report remains the official account of the assassination, and the most argued-over government inquiry in American history.
hotten-slang-1864:
John Camden Hotten issued his Slang Dictionary in 1864, the fullest record of Victorian street language. Hotten was a London publisher with a taste for the city's low life and its speech. He built the book on Grose's earlier slang dictionary and added the new words of his own century.

Inside are the cant of thieves, the patter of street sellers, and slang from schools, barracks, and music halls. Hotten explains terms that polite print of the day left out, often with notes on where a word came from. The result catches the English that Dickens put in his characters' mouths. For historians of speech and of city life, the dictionary is a first-hand record of a vanished London.
statesmans-yearbook-1864:
Frederick Martin edited the first Statesman's Year-Book in 1864, a compact survey of the world's states. Victorian readers faced a fast-changing map of new nations, wars, and empires, and Martin offered the facts in one yearly volume. The book was meant for officials, merchants, and anyone who needed to know how countries were run.

Each country gets a short account of its rulers, government, people, trade, money, and armed forces. The facts came from official returns and were revised for each new edition. The formula worked so well that the year-book is still published today, more than 160 years later. The first volume shows the world of 1864 as its own clerks and statesmen measured it.
cia-0000012364:
Through the summer of 1962 the Helms memos to the Director of Central Intelligence kept coming, this one dated July 2. The Penkovsky summit correspondence now ran toward the autumn of crisis. Paper flowed in both directions across the Potomac, questions down and answers up, while the colonel's fate hung over every page the file accumulated.

The two-way traffic shows a top fully engaged in a single case. Few sources in the agency's history held the summit's attention so long. For readers, the memo is one more proof of the channel's weight in the months before Cuba.
cia-0000013864: Someone saw a captured American officer in Phu Ly City, and a CIA note dated July 2, 1967, passes the sighting on. Phu Ly sits in Ha Nam Province, south of Hanoi. Sighting reports helped prove that a missing man was alive and in enemy hands. Each one gave his family and his service a fresh point on the map.
cia-0000014664: Reports from the field said Communists were capitalizing on something, in a CIA file dated November 1, 1952. The copy is marked poor, and the title itself is cut off. Even broken files were kept, since a scrap could matter later. This fragment shows the raw state of much Cold War reporting as it reached Washington desks.
cia-0000015264: Flying objects were seen in the Shakhty area, in a CIA report dated July 2, 1955. Shakhty was a coal town in the Soviet south. More than one object is claimed, which set the report apart from single light tales. The file adds a coal town's sky to the map of Soviet sightings.
cia-0000015464: East Germany had its own flying saucer reports, kept in a CIA record dated in 1952. The German Democratic Republic lay behind the Iron Curtain, where news was tightly held. Reports still leaked west and were filed in Washington. The entry shows the saucer wave crossing a hard border, with officials on one side trying to judge stories from the other.
cia-0000022364: Norway involuntarily became a party to American spy activity, a Soviet line kept in a CIA record dated in 1960. The heading adds a family angle that the catalog cuts short. Norway had been a planned landing ground in U-2 flight plans, which embarrassed Oslo. Moscow pressed that soreness hard, hoping to loosen a Western ally over the spy flights.
cia-0000022664: Photo comparison case number 12,769 has its results kept in a CIA record dated in 1971. The case sits one number below another result filed the same year. Numbered in the twelve thousands, these cases show the sheer scale of the picture matching effort. Behind each number stood a missing man, a family, and a folder of faces.
cia-0000028764: The situation and prospects in Cuba are judged in National Intelligence Estimate 85-2-62, dated in 1962. An NIE spoke for the whole intelligence community at the highest level. Cuba in 1962 meant Castro's state, Soviet ties, and, by autumn, the missile crisis. An estimate with that number is a landmark paper, read then by the men who faced the crisis.

A group of American pilots was allegedly held prisoner in a house, according to a CIA record dated May 1, 1983. The house stood near a place the title leaves cut short in the catalog. Most prisoner claims involved camps, which made a house an unusual detail.

Inside, the claim is recorded with the detail that made it stand out from the rest. Odd details could help a report, since a strange fact is harder to invent well. They could also hurt it, and analysts had to judge which way this one cut before the file could move forward.
cia-0000042864:
A communique was issued on the killings in El Salvador, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. A communique states an official position in set, careful words. The killings then at issue were those shaking the country that autumn.

Inside, the official wording is preserved exactly as released. Governments write such texts for foreign ears as much as for home ones. The file lets readers study the chosen phrases up close. What a communique leaves out can matter as much as what it says, and this one was read that way in every capital that received it.
cia-0000049064: El Salvador's minister of defense was reluctant to prosecute military officers, and a CIA item from 1983 records the reluctance. Prosecution was the one tool that could have broken the forces' habit of impunity, and the minister would not use it. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, naming the block at the top.

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1364:

frus-1945-50-intel-d64:

frus-1945-50-intel-d364:

frus-1861-d64:
From Washington on 29 July 1861, William H. Seward addressed a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 64 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A week after Bull Run, Seward's aim abroad was plain: no panic, no threats, no open door. This late July letter carries that aim to London. It shows a Secretary chastened by defeat at home but steady in his handling of the most risky front of the war. A week of such letters rebuilt abroad the calm that Bull Run had broken at home. Calm rebuilt abroad was worth regiments to a cause that had lost its first battle.
frus-1861-d164:
William Preston wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 May 1861. Preston had lately held the Madrid post for the United States. The dispatch is document 164 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Preston's letter comes from the handover season in Spain, as Schurz came to take the post. An outgoing envoy's report could still guide the new chief at home. His May page adds a Kentucky voice to the Spanish file of 1861. Preston, a Kentuckian of the old school, knew Spain from his years at its court. A clear thread in the whole volume runs through the hands of such aides.
frus-1861-d264:
30 October 1861 brought James Shepherd Pike a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 264 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d64:
15 May 1862 is the date on a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 64 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d164:
Dated 20 October 1862, Document 164 is a Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the State Department's yearly account of its work abroad during the Civil War.

The tempo of the London mail tells its own story: letters every few days, each one short and businesslike. Through them Washington tracked British shipyards building warships for the South, a sore point Adams raised again and again. This dispatch belongs to that grinding, vital strand of the wartime correspondence. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d264:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, opened April with a dispatch to William L. Dayton in Paris dated 1 April 1862, printed as Document 264 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

April 1862 would bring Shiloh's slaughter and the fall of New Orleans. Events that cut both ways in foreign eyes: proof of Union power and proof of the war's cost. Seward wrote at the month's start with his usual aim, to keep France from giving the South the one thing it lacked, a great-power friend. The letter starts the spring run of the Paris file. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d364:
Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 May 1862, in a letter printed as Document 364 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier wrote three weeks after his return from Richmond, where his April visit had stirred Union anger and Confederate hope. Relations between the minister and the Department were strained that spring. A letter from his hand in mid-May belongs to the repair and testing that followed. Both men were sounding out how much trust the channel still held. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862.
frus-1862-d464:
On 25 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to George Perkins Marsh, the American minister to Italy at Turin. The instruction is Document 464 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Marsh had spent the summer reporting Italian goodwill, and Seward's late-August order reached him as Union armies fell back in Virginia. Italy's government, still securing its new unity, had every reason to wish the Union well and little power to help it. Instructions to friendly but minor courts still mattered: they kept sympathy alive and denied Confederate agents any opening. The dispatch shows Seward tending the whole map of Europe, not just its great capitals, in a hard month.
frus-1862-d564:
On 14 January 1862 Henry Shelton Sanford reported from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward, five days after his previous dispatch. The report is Document 564 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Sanford's quick second letter of the year is characteristic: he wrote when he had something, not on a fixed day. Brussels gave him early word of moves in London and Paris, and January 1862 was full of moves, as Europe digested the Trent settlement. His reports fed Seward's sense of where the real dangers lay. The Belgian file's value lies in this flow of well-placed observation, offered by a minister who treated information as the whole of his job.
frus-1862-d664:

Direct notes like this one carried the formal voice of the United States to the shogun's court. They dealt in the courtesies and claims that held the young tie between the two lands in place. The letter is a rare formal piece in a file of working mail. It shows Washington treating Japan as a full partner in talks, not a mere port of call.
frus-1863p1-d64:
From the State Department on 26 January 1863 went this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 64 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, answering the thick mail Adams had sent that month.

Seward's letters did more than reply. They set the claims Adams was to press and the tone he was to use with Lord Russell. By early 1863 the two men had a rhythm: reports in by steamer, orders out by the next. This letter is one turn of that wheel, sent in the depths of a war winter.
frus-1863p1-d164:

The mate to a late-April letter held the day's last point for the London brief. Seward's pairs, all through this file, let each claim stand on its own page. He staffed it with paper as others staffed forts.
frus-1863p1-d264:
On 20 August 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. frus-1863p1-d364:
The British minister in Washington, Lord Lyons, took up his pen on 17 January 1863 to write Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is document 364 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. frus-1863p1-d464:
Dated 16 April 1863, document 464 is a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. plos-pbio-0020264:
Matteo Carandini examined trial-to-trial jitter in the visual brain in PLOS Biology in 2004. Show the same image twice, and neurons in the visual cortex fire a bit differently each time. That variability looks like noise, yet it grows in a set way as signals pass through the cortex.

The author shows that neurons amplify the jitter they receive, so variation builds stage by stage. That simple rule explains a lot of measured data. It also poses a puzzle: if the signal gets noisier, how does sight stay so steady? The answer likely lies in reading many neurons at once. The paper gives that debate a precise, testable base.
plos-pbio-0020364:
Paul Dassonville and Jagdeep Kaur Bala examined a visual illusion in PLOS Biology in 2004. In the Roelofs effect, a frame shifted to one side makes a centered target look off-center. People point wrong when asked where the target is, yet they can still act on its true place in some tests.

Some took that split as proof that perception and action use wholly separate vision systems. The authors argue the split is an illusion of testing, not of the brain. Their analysis urges care in how such effects are measured. The paper is a useful check on a famous claim, showing how a small task detail can mimic a deep divide in the mind.
plos-pone-0000064:
Eero Lindholm, Olle Melander, Peter Almgren, and a large team linked a gene variant to heart risk in PLOS ONE in 2006. The gene, MHC2TA, helps switch on immune genes. A variant in it was tied to features of the metabolic syndrome, a cluster that includes high blood sugar, blood pressure, and belly fat.

People with the variant also faced higher death rates from cardiovascular causes in the study group. A single gene touching both immune activity and metabolism is a plausible bridge between inflammation and heart disease. That bridge has become a major theme in heart research. The finding gives prevention work a marker to test in other populations.
plos-pone-0000164:
Junfeng Wu, Lixiang Xue, Mo Weng, and colleagues published this ageing study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It works with human diploid fibroblasts, normal connective tissue cells that stop dividing as they reach senescence, the worn-out state of old cells. The team shows that the protein Sp1 is essential for switching on the gene p16 INK4a during that process.

p16 INK4a is one of the main brakes that stops old cells from dividing, and it also guards against cancer. Tying that brake to Sp1 fills in a step of how cells enforce their own retirement. The finding matters for both ageing research and cancer biology, which share this pathway.
plos-pone-0000264:
Farid I. Kandil and Markus Lappe published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When the eyes take in a moving scene in fragments, the brain interpolates, filling the gaps across space and time to build one smooth view. The authors show this spatio-temporal interpolation is accomplished by binocular mechanisms that combine form and motion from both eyes.

Seeing a continuous world from two eyes and blinking, shifting inputs is a feat of reconstruction. The paper assigns that reconstruction to mechanisms that merge shape and movement. It helps explain how binocular vision stays stable and unified during natural viewing.
plos-pone-0000364:
Christina Lindqvist and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2007 on whether stress in parent chickens can shape their chicks. The team studied stress-caused learning problems and linked changes in brain gene activity, asking whether both can pass from one generation to the next.

The work treats learning ability and brain gene activity as traits that parental experience can influence before the chick is even hatched. Studies like this one test how much of an animal's early environment leaves marks that outlast a single lifetime. The findings bear on farming, animal welfare, and the biology of how traits are passed on outside of DNA sequence alone.
plos-pone-0000464:
Lise Denoeud and colleagues built a forecasting method for flu and pneumonia deaths, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Death records arrive slowly, but illness data, called morbidity data, are available sooner. The team tested whether those earlier signals can predict pneumonia and influenza mortality before the deaths are counted.

Timely mortality estimates help health officials judge an epidemic's severity while it is still unfolding, not after. A model that reads routine morbidity data could run every week at low cost. The work comes from France's long-running sentinel surveillance networks, an early example of the nowcasting methods now standard in public health.
plos-pone-0000564:
Shiping Zhang and colleagues identified a bacterial tail as essential armor against a lung protein, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterium that infects damaged lungs. Its flagellum, the rotating tail it swims with, is required for resistance to clearance. The clearer is surfactant protein A, a lung defense protein that helps sweep bacteria out.

The result is surprising: a swimming organ doubles as a shield. Losing the flagellum may slow the bacterium but expose it to clearance, a trade-off that shapes infection. Understanding such defenses helps explain why Pseudomonas is so hard to clear from the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients.
plos-pone-0000664:
Boel Brynedal, Kristina Duvefelt, Gudrun Jonasdottir and colleagues separated two genetic effects on multiple sclerosis risk, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A dense linkage screen had confirmed the HLA complex holds the strongest genetic factor for MS. A parallel analysis used 650 SNP markers across that complex to map the signal more finely.

Genes in the HLA region sit close together, so their effects are hard to untangle. The title reports that HLA-A influences MS risk independently of HLA-DRB1, the gene usually blamed first.
